methodology: Bull = (current fwd P/E x 1.20) x (consensus fwd EPS x 1.10). Conservative = (current fwd P/E x 0.70) x (consensus fwd EPS x 0.85). For Micron (deep cyclical) bull P/E uplift is 1.30 to reflect cycle re-rating.

companies.name: Palantir Technologies
companies.thesis: AIP (Artificial Intelligence Platform) commercial bookings continue to compound; US government remains sticky core. Picked because AIP is the clearest-monetizing AI software story among the large-caps and Q1 will test whether the 74% projected revenue growth and 115% EPS jump are baked in.
companies.macroAngle: Direct AI software beneficiary - if 'enterprise GenAI' goes from pilot to production, PLTR captures it.
companies.keyRisks: Valuation compression - any growth deceleration cuts deep at 110x fwd P/E.

financials.source: StockAnalysis financials, annual values in millions USD

dcf.note: High valuation and early AI software adoption make the terminal value very sensitive.

companies.name: Advanced Micro Devices
companies.thesis: MI355X/MI400 ramp + the multi-GW OpenAI supply agreement reframe AMD from 'NVDA also-ran' to credible #2 AI accelerator vendor. Picked because consensus EPS growth (+33% YoY) is high but achievable - and MI400 timing commentary on this print is the catalyst.
companies.macroAngle: AI chip shortage + customer concentration risk on NVDA = procurement teams are diversifying to AMD.
companies.keyRisks: Average analyst PT ($287) is below current price - market has already priced in the AI win. Miss = sharp re-rate.

financials.source: StockAnalysis financials, annual values in millions USD

dcf.note: AI GPU ramp and competitive share gains are still moving targets.

companies.name: Arm Holdings
companies.thesis: Royalty mix continues shifting to v9 (~2x rate of v8) and Arm-based data-center CPUs (NVDA Grace, AWS Graviton, Microsoft Cobalt) are scaling. Picked because every credible AI compute architecture pays Arm rent.
companies.macroAngle: Architecture moat - if AI compute keeps growing, royalty pool grows with it regardless of which chip vendor wins.
companies.keyRisks: Trades at 110x fwd - 220% above semi industry median. Any guidance softness is brutal.

financials.source: StockAnalysis financials, annual values in millions USD

dcf.note: Royalty model is high quality, but the current price depends heavily on very long-run growth.

companies.name: Arista Networks
companies.thesis: Leading switch silicon (Tomahawk-class) for AI back-end networks. Q1 consensus: rev ~$2.78B (+39% YoY), EPS ~$0.86. Picked because AI clusters need scale-out networking and ANET is the merchant-silicon leader vs Cisco's vertically-integrated stack.
companies.macroAngle: Every NVDA/AMD GPU cluster needs ANET-class fabric. The fastest-growing networking name in AI build-out.
companies.keyRisks: Customer concentration (Microsoft + Meta = ~40% of rev). Hyperscaler AI capex pause = revenue cliff. NVDA's Spectrum-X gaining traction.

financials.source: StockAnalysis financials, annual values in millions USD

dcf.note: Useful, but hyperscaler networking orders can be lumpy.

companies.name: Applied Materials
companies.thesis: Semicap leader benefiting from HBM and leading-edge logic capex. Q2 EPS guide $2.64 (annualized ~$10.50). Picked as picks-and-shovels for AI chip manufacturing - if MU/SK Hynix/Samsung build HBM capacity, AMAT sells the tools.
companies.macroAngle: TSMC + Intel + Samsung capex cycle is structurally up. AMAT, LRCX, KLAC are the three legs of equipment.
companies.keyRisks: China revenue exposure (~30%) + export controls. Memory capex is cyclical - Samsung HBM ramp pause = AMAT order softness.

financials.source: StockAnalysis financials, annual values in millions USD

dcf.note: Semicap orders are cyclical, so a single smooth DCF can misread the cycle.

companies.name: NVIDIA
companies.thesis: Blackwell at full ramp, Rubin disclosed for late 2026. Q1 FY27 will be the biggest AI tape of the year - data center revenue, China/H20 commentary, and Rubin lead-time guidance all matter. Despite size, fwd P/E of 24 is below most AI peers - the relative value within AI is here.
companies.macroAngle: Still the platform AI is built on. Networking (InfiniBand, Spectrum-X), CUDA, and full-stack systems = lock-in.
companies.keyRisks: Custom ASIC competition (AVGO/MRVL), China export controls, AMD MI400 traction.

financials.source: StockAnalysis financials, annual values in millions USD

dcf.note: Huge FCF makes DCF useful, but AI cycle assumptions dominate the result.

companies.name: Marvell Technology
companies.thesis: Custom AI silicon (Amazon Trainium 2/3, Microsoft Maia, Meta) + 800G/1.6T optical for AI fabrics. Smaller-cap competitor to AVGO with higher growth. April +67% rally on data center strength. Picked because MRVL is the 'AVGO option' play for AI ASICs.
companies.macroAngle: If hyperscalers keep building custom chips and AI optical interconnects scale, MRVL is a higher-beta way to express it.
companies.keyRisks: Average analyst PT ($128) is BELOW current price. Custom silicon design wins are lumpy (Trainium 3 timing). Optical competition from Coherent/CRDO.

financials.source: StockAnalysis financials, annual values in millions USD

dcf.note: Custom silicon design wins are lumpy, so the model is more directional than precise.

companies.name: Snowflake
companies.thesis: Cortex AI, Snowpark, and Iceberg interop are pulling enterprise AI workloads to the platform. Picked because AI training -> AI inference shift moves spend from GPU to data layer, where SNOW lives. Trades 44% below GuruFocus 'GF Value' - one of few AI infra names that screens cheap.
companies.macroAngle: Every AI agent/RAG app needs a query-able data layer. SNOW is positioned, but consumption-pricing means revenue is unlevered to user count.
companies.keyRisks: Negative GAAP op margins persist. Databricks competition. Consumption can compress in any IT-budget tightening.

financials.source: StockAnalysis financials, annual values in millions USD

dcf.note: Consumption revenue and reinvestment make near-term cash conversion less clean.

companies.name: Dell Technologies
companies.thesis: Q1 FY27 guide: rev $34.7-35.7B (+51% YoY) with ~$13B AI server revenue and $43B AI backlog. Picked because DELL is the cheapest large-cap (16x fwd) direct AI infra play - profitable, dividend-paying, buying back stock.
companies.macroAngle: Hyperscalers buy from NVDA, Tier-2 enterprises and sovereign AI buy from DELL. The AI build-out is broadening to enterprise.

health.balance: Debt heavy but serviced by FCF

companies.keyRisks: AI server margins are thin (~7-10% vs NVDA 75%). Backlog concentration in 1-2 customers (xAI). PC business drag offsetting AI mix gains.

financials.source: StockAnalysis financials, annual values in millions USD

dcf.note: Cash flow is easier to model, but hardware margins and AI server mix still matter.

companies.name: MongoDB
companies.thesis: Atlas Vector Search + native vector indexing positions MDB as the 'AI-native' transactional DB. FY27 guidance: Q1 EPS $1.32 climbing to Q4 $1.81 (~$6.30 annual). Picked because vector DBs are the storage layer for RAG/agent applications.
companies.macroAngle: Every production AI app needs a vector DB. MDB has document + vector in one system, no Pinecone/Weaviate sidecar.
companies.keyRisks: TTM EPS still negative - profitability inflection unproven. Postgres + pgvector is a credible alternative. Atlas growth deceleration was a 2H25 concern.

financials.source: StockAnalysis financials, annual values in millions USD

dcf.note: Profitability is still developing, so DCF depends on margin expansion assumptions.

companies.name: Broadcom
companies.thesis: Custom AI silicon for hyperscalers (Google TPU, Meta MTIA, rumored OpenAI) + Tomahawk/Jericho networking. Picked because custom ASICs are the credible alternative when a hyperscaler doesn't want to pay NVDA's margin. Steady FCF + AI growth = lower-vol way to own the theme.
companies.macroAngle: If 'every hyperscaler builds custom AI chips' is the future, AVGO is the pick-and-shovel.

health.balance: Significant debt (~$70B) from VMware deal but covered by FCF

companies.keyRisks: VMware integration, leverage. Custom ASIC visibility is lumpy by hyperscaler design cycle.

financials.source: StockAnalysis financials, annual values in millions USD

dcf.note: Strong FCF supports DCF, though VMware debt and AI ASIC cycle visibility matter.

companies.name: CrowdStrike Holdings
companies.thesis: Falcon AI/Charlotte AI driving module attach; July 2024 outage scar largely healed in NRR. Picked because AI security is an emerging $30B+ TAM and CRWD's platform pricing > point-product peers.
companies.macroAngle: AI agents creating new attack surface = endpoint/identity security spend keeps growing.
companies.keyRisks: 94x fwd P/E vs software median 18x. Customer commitment package discounts post-outage compress NRR. SentinelOne / Microsoft E5 competition.

financials.source: StockAnalysis financials, annual values in millions USD

dcf.note: Recurring revenue helps, but valuation is still highly sensitive to growth duration.

companies.name: Adobe
companies.thesis: 10.6x fwd P/E (42.8% BELOW software median) reflects fear that GenAI commoditizes creative tools. But Firefly + GenStudio + Acrobat AI Assistant are monetizing. Picked as the ASYMMETRIC value play - if AI cannibalization fears prove overstated, multiple expansion is dramatic.
companies.macroAngle: The bear case (Midjourney/Sora kill Photoshop) vs bull case (Adobe wins enterprise AI creative) is the definitional AI software fight of 2026.

financials.source: StockAnalysis financials, annual values in millions USD

companies.keyRisks: Net New ARR deceleration is the metric to watch. Figma re-emerged as a competitor post-failed-acquisition. Generative AI tooling commoditization fear isn't priced in fully if revenue slows.

dcf.note: One of the cleaner DCF names: mature software, high margins, and steady FCF.

companies.name: Oracle
companies.thesis: OCI re-rated as AI training/inference cloud after the multi-deca-billion OpenAI/Stargate-related RPO step-ups in 2H25. Picked because ORCL is the cheapest large-cap way (21x fwd) to own AI cloud capex - and FY26 capex visibility on this print is the catalyst.
companies.macroAngle: Capex shifting from hyperscalers to ORCL = AI infra winner with margin upside as utilization climbs.
companies.keyRisks: FCF turning negative as AI capex front-loads. Customer concentration in OpenAI/RPO contracts. Execution on GPU procurement.

financials.source: StockAnalysis financials, annual values in millions USD

dcf.note: Mature base supports DCF, but AI cloud capex can depress near-term FCF.

companies.name: Micron Technology
companies.thesis: Sole American HBM supplier; 2026 HBM capacity is sold out at agreed price/volume incl. HBM4. Picked because forward earnings estimates have reset sharply higher while HBM supply remains tight. The stock has already re-rated, so the next print has to prove the memory cycle can stay stronger for longer.
companies.macroAngle: HBM TAM ~$35B (2025) -> ~$100B (2028). Direct beneficiary of every NVDA/AMD/custom-ASIC unit shipped.
companies.keyRisks: DRAM cyclicality - peak-margin assumptions are often wrong at the top. Samsung HBM3E qualification at NVDA could compress price.

financials.source: StockAnalysis financials, annual values in millions USD

dcf.note: Memory is deeply cyclical. DCF can be misleading at cycle peaks and troughs.

companies.name: Microsoft
companies.thesis: Azure OpenAI + M365 Copilot + Maia custom silicon make MSFT the most direct large-cap beneficiary of enterprise AI spend. The Q4 FY26 print (late July) is the read on whether Azure AI growth is still holding while ~$80B+ of FY26 capex front-loads into FY27. Picked because at 22x fwd P/E it is the cheapest 'platform AI' name despite carrying the largest absolute AI revenue base.
companies.macroAngle: If enterprise AI moves from pilot to production at scale, MSFT captures it across Azure consumption, Copilot seats, GitHub, and search/ads. It owns both the platform and the apps.

health.balance: $78B cash, $125B debt; FCF easily services it

companies.keyRisks: AI capex (~$80B+ annual run-rate) compressing FCF margin even as revenue grows. OpenAI relationship/economics ambiguity. Azure AI growth deceleration would re-rate quickly given the size.

financials.source: StockAnalysis financials, annual values in millions USD; FY ends June 30

dcf.note: Earnings are mature and very visible, but heavy AI capex (~$80B+ annual) is compressing near-term FCF/EPS conversion.

companies.name: Intel
companies.thesis: Turnaround story stock - the rally from sub-$20 a year ago to ~$100 prices in 18A foundry traction (rumored external customer wins) and Gaudi 3 finding pocket share in the AI accelerator stack. But TTM EPS is still negative and FCF is roughly -$3B. Picked because Q2 print is the first real test of whether the multiple can hold without earnings catching up.
companies.macroAngle: If a US foundry alternative to TSMC matters for AI supply chain (and US policy keeps paying for that to happen), INTC is the only credible bet. The thesis lives or dies on 18A yields and external customer wins.

health.balance: $33B cash, $45B debt; dividend suspended in FY25

companies.keyRisks: Average analyst PT ($65) is ~35% BELOW current price - sell-side does not believe the rally. 18A yield disappointment, external customer-win delay, or any FCF backslide is brutal at 96x fwd P/E. Trailing EPS still negative.

profitability.source: StockAnalysis statistics, crawled May 2026; FCF margin computed from FY25 financials

financials.source: StockAnalysis financials, annual values in millions USD

dcf.note: TTM EPS is still negative and FCF is negative. Any DCF here is essentially a bet on margin and 18A foundry recovery, not a read on current cash flow.

companies.name: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing
companies.thesis: Every advanced AI chip — NVIDIA, AMD, Apple, Google TPU — is manufactured by TSMC. No other foundry can make 3nm/2nm at scale. AI demand is forcing TSMC to expand aggressively in Arizona and Japan. Picked because TSMC is the single most irreplaceable company in the entire AI supply chain; you cannot build AI hardware without them.
companies.macroAngle: AI capex supercycle flows directly into TSMC wafer demand. Every dollar hyperscalers spend on AI chips is revenue for TSMC.

health.balance: Net cash position, no financial stress

companies.keyRisks: Geopolitical risk (Taiwan Strait); US tariff uncertainty on Taiwan exports; customer concentration in NVIDIA/Apple.

financials.source: Approximate in millions USD, to be updated from StockAnalysis

dcf.note: Capex-heavy foundry model compresses near-term FCF but long-run moat is unmatched. DCF understates strategic value.

companies.name: ASML Holding
companies.thesis: ASML is the only company in the world that makes EUV lithography machines — the equipment that physically prints the circuits on advanced chips. Without ASML, TSMC, Samsung, and Intel cannot manufacture cutting-edge AI chips. This absolute monopoly on EUV makes ASML the deepest moat in the entire semiconductor industry. Picked because it is a geopolitical chokepoint (US uses it as an export control lever) and has a decade-long order backlog.
companies.macroAngle: Every new AI chip fab requires ASML EUV machines. Hyperscaler AI capex creates multi-year equipment demand regardless of chip brand competition.

health.balance: Minimal debt, strong EUR cash generation

companies.keyRisks: China export restrictions (30%+ of revenue at risk); lumpy order book can cause quarterly misses; EUR/USD FX headwind.

financials.source: Approximate in millions EUR converted to USD, to be updated

dcf.note: Monopoly EUV position justifies premium terminal multiple. Export control risk is the key DCF wildcard.

companies.name: Lam Research
companies.thesis: Lam Research makes the etch and deposition equipment that creates the layered 3D structures inside NAND flash and logic chips. As AI drives demand for more HBM and advanced NAND, Lam is a direct beneficiary — every new wafer fab needs Lam tools. Picked because it is a picks-and-shovels play that earns revenue on equipment AND recurring services/spares, making it more resilient than chip designers mid-cycle.
companies.macroAngle: AI infrastructure buildout requires new chip fabs; fab construction spending = equipment orders for Lam.
companies.keyRisks: China export restrictions; WFE (wafer fab equipment) spending cycles can compress sharply in downturns.

financials.source: Approximate in millions USD, to be updated

dcf.note: Cyclical equipment company; DCF sensitive to WFE spending assumptions.

companies.name: KLA Corporation
companies.thesis: KLA makes the inspection and metrology tools that catch defects during chip manufacturing — you cannot yield high-quality advanced chips without KLA's process control equipment. As chips get smaller and more complex (for AI), defect tolerance shrinks and KLA's tools become more critical, not less. Picked because KLA has the highest gross margins in semiconductor equipment (~60%), recurring service revenue, and benefits proportionally MORE as chip complexity increases.
companies.macroAngle: Tighter chip geometries for AI accelerators = more KLA tools per wafer. Process control spending is non-discretionary once a fab is running.

health.balance: Moderate leverage, strong cash generation, consistent buybacks

companies.keyRisks: China export controls; WFE spending cycle downturn; customer concentration at TSMC/Samsung/Intel.

financials.source: Approximate in millions USD, to be updated

dcf.note: Best FCF margins in equipment sector; less cyclical than peers due to process control necessity.

companies.name: Qualcomm
companies.thesis: Qualcomm's Snapdragon chips power the majority of premium Android phones and Windows Copilot+ PCs — the devices where on-device AI inference is being deployed at scale. As AI moves from the cloud to the edge (faster, private, no latency), Qualcomm's NPU (neural processing unit) technology is the key enabler. Picked because Qualcomm is deeply undervalued relative to the AI edge opportunity and trades at a significant discount to NVIDIA despite being the dominant AI chip for mobile/PC.
companies.macroAngle: AI inference shifting to edge devices = every phone upgrade and PC refresh is a Qualcomm win. Also expanding into automotive AI.

health.balance: Moderate debt, significant cash, strong dividend + buybacks

companies.keyRisks: Apple custom modem threatens long-term iPhone modem revenue; China revenue exposure (~60% of sales); licensing IP disputes.

financials.source: Approximate in millions USD, to be updated

dcf.note: Undervalued relative to peers; licensing revenue provides floor; edge AI expansion is upside.

companies.name: Amazon
companies.thesis: AWS is the world's largest cloud platform and is embedding AI at every layer — from foundation model hosting (Bedrock) to custom AI chips (Trainium for training, Inferentia for inference) designed to offer lower-cost alternatives to NVIDIA GPUs. Amazon is also deploying AI aggressively across its own retail and logistics operations. Picked because AWS AI services are growing faster than overall cloud, and Amazon's custom silicon strategy could reduce NVIDIA dependency and expand margins structurally.
companies.macroAngle: Enterprise cloud migration + AI workload shift = durable AWS growth. Every enterprise AI deployment needs a cloud platform; AWS is #1.
companies.keyRisks: AWS growth deceleration; antitrust regulatory risk; retail margin compression; high capex for AI buildout.

financials.source: Approximate in millions USD, to be updated

dcf.note: AWS operating leverage drives long-term FCF expansion. Retail segment adds complexity to DCF.

companies.name: Alphabet
companies.thesis: Alphabet operates the world's most valuable AI asset — Google Search — while simultaneously building the full AI stack: Gemini models, TPU custom chips, Google Cloud (GCP) AI services, and DeepMind research. Google Cloud is the fastest-growing hyperscaler segment. Picked because Alphabet is arguably the most undervalued among the mega-cap AI names at ~19x forward earnings, yet owns more AI infrastructure and research talent than almost any other company.
companies.macroAngle: AI-enhanced Search protects the $200B+ advertising moat; GCP AI services are a second growth engine with higher margins than ads.
companies.keyRisks: AI disruption to Search ad model (ChatGPT/Perplexity); antitrust breakup risk; high AI capex consuming FCF.

financials.source: Approximate in millions USD, to be updated

dcf.note: High FCF yield for a mega-cap AI company; Search moat provides durable base while GCP is the growth kicker.

companies.name: Meta Platforms
companies.thesis: Meta is spending more on AI infrastructure than any other company in absolute dollar terms ($60B+ capex in 2025) while simultaneously open-sourcing LLaMA models to commoditize the AI stack below its ad platform. This aggressive AI investment is already paying off: AI-driven ad targeting improvements have been cited as a key driver of 20%+ revenue growth. Picked because Meta combines the highest AI capex commitment with one of the most profitable underlying businesses (55%+ operating margins on ads).
companies.macroAngle: AI-powered ad personalization = more revenue per user. Every 1% improvement in ad relevance is billions in incremental revenue at Meta's scale.
companies.keyRisks: Regulatory risk (EU, FTC); Reality Labs losses ($20B+/yr) burning cash; AI capex overhang if ROI disappoints.

financials.source: Approximate in millions USD, to be updated

dcf.note: Strong FCF but capex surge compresses near-term FCF; terminal value depends on AI monetization success.

companies.name: Vertiv Holdings
companies.thesis: Vertiv makes the power distribution, UPS systems, and liquid cooling infrastructure that data centers physically require to run AI workloads. AI GPU clusters consume 5-10x more power per rack than traditional servers, creating a massive upgrade cycle for Vertiv's products. Picked because Vertiv is the most direct pure-play on the data center power/cooling bottleneck — hyperscalers cannot physically run more AI without Vertiv's equipment, and the order backlog is multi-year.
companies.macroAngle: Every AI data center built requires power and cooling infrastructure. AI's energy density is forcing a full replacement cycle for legacy thermal management.

health.balance: Moderate leverage from LBO history, deleveraging rapidly

companies.keyRisks: High valuation; data center capex slowdown risk; execution risk on rapid scaling; competition from Eaton and Schneider Electric.

financials.source: Approximate in millions USD, to be updated

dcf.note: High growth rate justified by AI data center buildout supercycle; leverage adds risk to downside.

companies.name: Super Micro Computer
companies.thesis: Super Micro is NVIDIA's primary rack-scale integration partner — they take NVIDIA GPUs and build the full server systems (GPU clusters, liquid-cooled racks) that hyperscalers and enterprises actually deploy. SMCI's modular 'building block' architecture allows rapid product iteration as new GPUs launch. Picked as a high-beta, direct-line-of-sight play on NVIDIA GPU deployment volume — if NVIDIA ships more H100/B200, SMCI builds the servers.
companies.macroAngle: AI capex = GPU server purchases = SMCI revenue. Direct correlation to NVIDIA shipment volumes.

health.balance: Manageable debt; recent accounting controversy resolved

companies.keyRisks: Accounting/audit controversy overhang; thin margins leave little buffer; customer concentration; inventory risk on GPU transitions.

financials.source: Approximate in millions USD, to be updated

dcf.note: Thin margins and accounting overhang make DCF unreliable; better valued on P/S or EV/Revenue.

companies.name: Equinix
companies.thesis: Equinix owns and operates 260+ carrier-neutral data centers across 33 countries — the physical hubs where internet traffic, enterprise workloads, and increasingly AI inference workloads are colocated and interconnected. Its Fabric platform allows direct private connectivity between clouds, enterprises, and AI services. Picked because Equinix benefits from AI demand while offering a more defensive, REIT-like cash flow profile than pure-play AI growth stocks — it has raised dividends for 10+ consecutive years.
companies.macroAngle: AI inference must run close to users globally; Equinix's network of neutral data centers is the preferred deployment site for low-latency AI services.

health.balance: REIT structure; higher leverage is normal; investment-grade rated

companies.keyRisks: High capex for expansion; interest rate sensitivity as a REIT; power availability constraints in key markets.

financials.source: Approximate in millions USD, to be updated

dcf.note: REIT; value better captured through AFFO yield and dividend growth than pure FCF DCF.

companies.name: Vistra Corp
companies.thesis: AI data centers consume enormous amounts of electricity 24/7, and Vistra is one of the largest independent power producers in the US with a large nuclear fleet that provides always-on, carbon-free power — exactly what hyperscalers want. Vistra's Illinois and Texas nuclear plants are ideally positioned to sign long-term power purchase agreements (PPAs) with tech giants. Picked because Vistra is a non-obvious AI play that benefits from the power demand surge without the chip-cycle volatility.
companies.macroAngle: AI electricity demand = power price appreciation = higher margins for all power producers, but nuclear and clean baseload command a premium.
companies.keyRisks: Power price volatility; regulatory/nuclear policy risk; high leverage; weather impacts on generation.

financials.source: Approximate in millions USD, to be updated

dcf.note: Power market volatility makes terminal assumptions difficult; nuclear PPA pipeline is key upside driver.

companies.name: Constellation Energy
companies.subTheme: Nuclear Power for AI Data Centers
companies.thesis: Constellation is the largest nuclear power operator in the US and signed a landmark 20-year, $1.6B/yr power purchase agreement with Microsoft to restart the Three Mile Island nuclear plant specifically to power AI data centers. This deal validated the nuclear-AI thesis and triggered similar deals across the sector. Picked because Constellation has the largest clean baseload power portfolio for hyperscaler AI PPAs, pricing in long-term contracted revenue streams that trade at a discount to what they are worth.
companies.macroAngle: Hyperscalers need 24/7 clean power for AI and have made public net-zero pledges; nuclear is the only technology that satisfies both — Constellation is the primary supplier.
companies.keyRisks: Nuclear regulatory and safety risk; political/policy risk on nuclear subsidies; power price exposure for uncontracted output.

financials.source: Approximate in millions USD, to be updated

dcf.note: Long-term contracted PPA revenue de-risks cash flows; Microsoft 20yr deal anchors valuation floor.

companies.name: Coherent Corp
companies.thesis: Inside AI data centers, massive amounts of data move between GPU clusters at extreme speeds — this requires optical transceivers (converts electrical signals to light for fiber transmission). Coherent is one of the two dominant suppliers of these 400G/800G optical transceiver modules. As AI clusters scale to thousands of GPUs, networking costs become a bottleneck and optical interconnects are the solution. Picked because Coherent is a direct, underfollowed beneficiary of GPU cluster networking demand.
companies.macroAngle: More GPUs per cluster = more networking bandwidth needed = more optical transceivers. NVIDIA's NVLink and InfiniBand networking both require optical components at scale.

health.balance: Higher leverage from II-VI merger acquisition; deleveraging in progress

companies.keyRisks: High leverage from merger; competition from Lumentum and Inphi; gross margin recovery pace.

financials.source: Approximate in millions USD, to be updated

dcf.note: Leverage and recent losses make DCF unreliable near-term; EV/EBITDA or EV/Revenue more appropriate.

companies.name: Cloudflare
companies.thesis: Cloudflare has built a global network of 300+ points of presence (PoPs) that now doubles as a distributed AI inference network through its Workers AI platform — developers can run AI models at the edge, close to users, with minimal latency. This positions Cloudflare as an alternative to AWS/Azure/GCP for AI inference at scale without the data center. Picked because Cloudflare is quietly becoming the dominant edge computing and AI inference platform with enterprise security bundled in, and the TAM expansion from AI is significant.
companies.macroAngle: AI inference shifting to edge = Cloudflare's network becomes the preferred deployment platform for latency-sensitive AI applications.
companies.keyRisks: High valuation; competition from AWS CloudFront and Fastly; GAAP profitability still thin; stock-based comp dilution.

financials.source: Approximate in millions USD, to be updated

dcf.note: High growth but expensive; terminal value very sensitive to margin expansion assumptions.

companies.name: ServiceNow
companies.thesis: ServiceNow is embedding AI (called Now Assist) into its dominant IT Service Management platform, enabling companies to automate workflows, resolve IT tickets, and manage enterprise operations with AI agents. Every large enterprise runs ServiceNow, and AI is becoming the primary upsell vector that is expanding deal sizes by 30-50%. Picked because ServiceNow has a captive, sticky enterprise customer base to cross-sell AI into, a 99%+ renewal rate, and is one of the clearest enterprise AI monetization stories.
companies.macroAngle: Enterprises adopting AI agents = they need an orchestration and workflow layer — ServiceNow's platform is the natural home for enterprise AI agents.
companies.keyRisks: Valuation risk at 55x forward; competition from Microsoft Copilot in enterprise; economic slowdown cuts IT budgets.

financials.source: Approximate in millions USD, to be updated

dcf.note: High quality FCF compounder; valuation is premium but justified by durable enterprise switching costs.

companies.name: Salesforce
companies.thesis: Salesforce launched Agentforce — a platform for deploying autonomous AI agents that handle sales, service, and marketing tasks within its CRM ecosystem. With 150,000+ enterprise customers deeply embedded in Salesforce's platform, Agentforce has an unmatched distribution channel for enterprise AI agent adoption. Picked because Salesforce is one of the few companies that can monetize AI agents at enterprise scale immediately — existing customers simply add AI agent seats on top of their existing contracts.
companies.macroAngle: Enterprise AI agent adoption is accelerating; Salesforce owns the CRM relationships where most enterprise AI agents will first be deployed.

health.balance: Net cash; active buybacks and dividend initiated

companies.keyRisks: Slower-than-expected Agentforce adoption; competition from Microsoft Copilot; organic growth deceleration post-Slack/Tableau integrations.

financials.source: Approximate in millions USD, to be updated

dcf.note: Very high FCF yield for an AI software compounder; Agentforce is the near-term growth catalyst.

companies.name: Datadog
companies.thesis: As enterprises build and deploy AI applications, they need to monitor, debug, and optimize those AI workloads — Datadog's LLM Observability product does exactly this. Datadog is already the dominant cloud monitoring platform and AI workloads generate significantly more observability data than traditional apps, expanding consumption. Picked because Datadog earns more revenue as AI applications become more complex — it is a usage-based model where AI is inherently a tailwind, not a threat.
companies.macroAngle: More AI workloads = more monitoring data = more Datadog consumption. AI is Datadog's most powerful secular tailwind.
companies.keyRisks: Valuation; competition from Dynatrace and New Relic; macro-driven cloud cost optimization pressure.

financials.source: Approximate in millions USD, to be updated

dcf.note: Premium growth rate justified by usage-based AI tailwind; expensive but high-quality compounder.

companies.name: Pure Storage
companies.thesis: AI training requires reading and writing massive datasets at extremely high throughput speeds — spinning hard drives cannot keep up. Pure Storage's all-flash arrays (DirectFlash) are purpose-built for the random-access, high-bandwidth patterns of AI training and inference. Pure has won major AI lab and hyperscaler storage contracts specifically because NAND flash is the only technology that can feed GPUs fast enough. Picked because Pure Storage is the clearest pure-play on AI storage infrastructure, an often-overlooked bottleneck.
companies.macroAngle: AI training jobs are I/O bound; faster storage = higher GPU utilization = less wasted compute time. AI customers pay premium for Pure's performance.
companies.keyRisks: Competition from NetApp and Dell; commoditization of flash storage; customer concentration in hyperscalers.

financials.source: Approximate in millions USD, to be updated

dcf.note: FCF positive and growing; AI storage is structural tailwind; reasonable valuation for the growth profile.

companies.name: Western Digital
companies.thesis: Western Digital (parent of SanDisk NAND brand, spun off Feb 2025) makes HDDs and flash storage that underpin the massive data lakes AI models are trained on. While not glamorous, AI training requires petabytes of raw storage capacity at low cost — WDC's HDDs remain the cheapest per-terabyte storage option. The HDD business is also rebounding as nearline (high-capacity data center) HDDs see strong demand from AI data archival. Picked as a value-oriented way to capture AI storage demand at a significant discount to pure-play AI names.
companies.macroAngle: AI training datasets are enormous and growing; cheap bulk storage (HDD) is the foundation of every AI company's data infrastructure.

health.balance: Moderate leverage, improving as cycle turns

companies.keyRisks: HDD demand highly cyclical; NAND oversupply risk; WDC/SanDisk post-spinoff execution; competition from Seagate.

financials.source: Approximate in millions USD, to be updated

dcf.note: Deep cyclical; DCF highly sensitive to cycle timing. Better valued on P/B or EV/EBITDA at cycle trough.

broaderWatchlist.name: Apple
broaderWatchlist.thesis: Apple is here as a quality compounder watch, not an AI-pure-play. The reason to track it is simple: huge installed base, services margin, buybacks, and very large free cash flow. The current debate is whether iPhone/Mac demand and Apple Intelligence can restart growth enough to justify the premium multiple.
broaderWatchlist.macroAngle: Broader watch angle: consumer hardware demand, services durability, memory cost pressure, and whether Apple can close the perceived AI gap without hurting margins.
broaderWatchlist.keyRisks: Valuation is already rich for a slower-growth mega-cap. China demand, App Store regulation, memory/component inflation, and delayed AI execution can pressure both revenue growth and the multiple.

financials.source: StockAnalysis financials, annual values in millions USD

dcf.note: AAPL is one of the cleaner DCF names because cash flow, buybacks, and margins are mature and visible.

broaderWatchlist.name: Tesla
broaderWatchlist.thesis: Tesla is a high-beta story stock. The dashboard should track whether the core EV business is stabilizing while the market keeps paying for robotaxi, autonomy, energy storage, and robotics optionality. It is not cheap on current earnings, so delivery growth and margin recovery matter a lot.
broaderWatchlist.macroAngle: Broader watch angle: EV demand, price cuts, battery costs, autonomous driving regulation, and whether non-car businesses can support the valuation.
broaderWatchlist.keyRisks: Current earnings do not support the full valuation without major future optionality. EV competition, margin compression, regulatory risk, execution delays, and CEO/key-person risk can move the stock sharply.

financials.source: StockAnalysis financials, annual values in millions USD

dcf.note: TSLA DCF is highly assumption-driven because much of the market value depends on future optionality, not current cash flow.

broaderWatchlist.name: Grab Holdings
broaderWatchlist.thesis: Grab is a regional growth and profitability watch. The reason to track it is whether mobility, delivery, fintech, and advertising can keep compounding while the company turns accounting profit into durable free cash flow. The balance sheet gives it room, but cash conversion is the key proof point.
broaderWatchlist.macroAngle: Broader watch angle: Southeast Asia consumer demand, take-rate expansion, fintech losses, competition intensity, and whether incentives/subsidies stay disciplined.
broaderWatchlist.keyRisks: Competition in delivery and ride-hailing can force subsidies back up. Fintech credit risk, regulation, FX moves, and weak free cash flow can keep the stock volatile even if revenue grows.

financials.source: StockAnalysis financials, annual values in millions USD

dcf.note: GRAB is becoming profitable, but the model is still sensitive to cash conversion and reinvestment assumptions.

broaderWatchlist.name: Unity Software
broaderWatchlist.thesis: Unity is a turnaround watch. The core question is whether the company can rebuild developer trust, stabilize Create, and make the ad/monetization business grow again after restructuring. It has real platform value, but the proof needs to show up in revenue quality and free cash flow.
broaderWatchlist.macroAngle: Broader watch angle: gaming demand, AI-generated content risk, ad-tech recovery, cost discipline, and whether Unity can grow without damaging its developer ecosystem.
broaderWatchlist.keyRisks: Turnaround execution is the risk. Revenue can remain choppy, AI tools may pressure game-engine value, and past pricing/trust issues can slow adoption. The company still reports negative GAAP earnings.

financials.source: StockAnalysis financials, annual values in millions USD

dcf.note: Unity has cash-flow potential, but a DCF depends heavily on margin recovery and sustained product trust.

broaderWatchlist.name: Alibaba Group
broaderWatchlist.thesis: Alibaba is a broader platform watch, not an AI pure-play. The core business is still China commerce, international e-commerce, local services, logistics, and cloud. The AI angle is real through Alibaba Cloud and Qwen, but the stock will still be driven by China consumer demand, competitive intensity, cloud growth, and whether AI spending converts into profitable revenue.
broaderWatchlist.macroAngle: Broader watch angle: China consumer recovery, cloud AI adoption, Qwen/model monetization, US-China restrictions, ADR sentiment, and whether higher AI infrastructure capex becomes durable cloud profit rather than just lower near-term free cash flow.
broaderWatchlist.keyRisks: China macro weakness, e-commerce and local-services price competition, regulatory/geopolitical risk, ADR sentiment, export controls, and heavy AI/cloud capex can all pressure margins and free cash flow.

financials.source: StockAnalysis financials, annual values converted from CNY to approximate millions USD

dcf.note: Alibaba generates real cash flow, but China macro risk, ADR/geopolitical risk, and AI cloud capex make the DCF more fragile than mature US mega-cap software names.
